Executive Overview: Design Technology Sequence

Overview & Purpose

The Design Technology I & II sequence establishes the sophomore-level technological foundation for graphic design. Replacing the legacy "isolated software/tutorial" model, this sequence positions technology as an active design medium — framing it as the study of how information is structured, translated, produced, and made responsive across media.

Students move from managing file infrastructure to building scalable systems, developing durable habits in production literacy, web accessibility, systems thinking, and emerging AI workflows.

Position Statement

Design Technology is the study of how information is structured, translated, produced, and made responsive across media.

Regardless of specialization, contemporary designers work within complex technological systems. To design effectively across publications, interfaces, environments, or emerging media, students must understand how information behaves across varied platforms, formats, and contexts.

Broad View of Technology

Technology spans material, production, information, communication, and computational systems — from paper, typography, and web standards to design systems, component libraries, and AI-assisted workflows.

Critical Understanding

Technologies are never neutral; each carries inherent assumptions, defaults, and constraints that shape design outcomes. The goal is not software mastery for its own sake, but using technology as a vehicle to understand design deeply.

Core Capabilities

Students learn to:

  • Understand media and production constraints.
  • Translate information seamlessly across formats.
  • Build structured, scalable systems and responsive experiences.
  • Critically engage emerging tools and adapt to future workflows.

Format & Delivery Model

To balance conceptual rigor with hands-on execution, both courses utilize a high-impact Lecture / Lab Orchestration Model:

  • Lecture / Orchestrator (1 hr 10 min): Cohort-wide instructional session focused on core concepts, systems thinking, design history/ethics, technical logic, and live methodology demonstrations.
  • Studio / Breakout Orientator (50 min): Immediate hands-on breakout lab focused on tactical application, troubleshooting, peer critique, and guided project execution.

This structure ensures students move immediately from conceptual understanding to applied execution, eliminating passive tutorial consumption.

Architecture & Units

Sequence Arc

DT I DT II
Media Systems
Translation Interaction
Output Behavior
Structure Responsiveness

Sequence Progression

Semester Core Focus Concepts Student Outcome
Design Technology I Media + Translation + Output Structure, Translation, Format, Technical Literacy Students design across media.
Design Technology II Systems + Interaction + Behavior Components, Responsiveness, Prototyping, Time Students design systems across time.

Design Technology I

  • Focus: Media, Translation, & Output
  • Core Shift: Moving from static software usage to understanding technological environments, print/digital constraints, and structured markup.
Unit Topics & Conceptual Rigor Assessment / Deliverable
Unit 1: Digital Foundations File structures, metadata, cloud/local OS mechanics, font licensing ethics, versioning. Asset System Setup: Standardized, scalable cloud/Local folder architecture following strict naming protocols.
Unit 2: Media & Translation Resolution calculations (300 dpi vs. 72 dpi), color spaces (CMYK/Pantone vs. RGB/Hex), substrates, ink limits. Cross-Media Package: Translated visual system as print-ready packaged vector/raster files and web graphics.
Unit 3: Publication & Info Systems Typographic grids, modular scales, baseline grids, master pages, paragraph/character styles. Multi-Page Publication System: Multi-page layout in InDesign enforcing structural grid hierarchy and automated style sheets.
Unit 4: Structured Screen Media Semantic HTML5, CSS Grid/Flexbox, WCAG accessibility standards (contrast, alt tags), fluid typography. Responsive Front-End Build: Functional, multi-page HTML/CSS site translating the Unit 3 publication layout to screen.

Design Technology II

  • Focus: Systems, Interaction, & Behavior
  • Core Shift: Moving from fixed media to dynamic, scalable, responsive, and generative systems.
Unit Topics & Conceptual Rigor Assessment / Deliverable
Unit 1: Interaction Foundations Information architecture (IA), user journey mapping, task flows, UX usability heuristics, wireframing. IA & Process Book: Complete low-to-mid fidelity wireframes, user journeys, and usability test results for a complex task.
Unit 2: Components & Design Systems Atomic design, Figma variables, design tokens, auto-layout, system governance, handoff documentation. Scalable UI Kit & Token Library: Documented, nested component system with global variables for light/dark modes.
Unit 3: Motion & Behavior Micro-interactions, temporal transitions, state changes, affordances, feedback loops. Interactive Motion Prototype: High-fidelity prototype showcasing complex component state transitions and motion choreography.
Unit 4: Responsive & Generative Systems Dynamic layouts, API integration, multi-breakpoint design, AI workflow bias/ethics, graceful degradation. Responsive/Generative Environment: Multi-breakpoint prototype using dynamic content/APIs, paired with an ethical audit essay.

Longitudinal Integration

Junior/Senior Level Reiteration

To maintain technical currency across the upper-division studio curriculum without adding credit bloat, concepts from ArtGr 2750/2760 can be reinforced through two proposed strategies:

Option A: The 1-Credit "Technology Module" (Recurring Lab)

  • Format: A 1-credit, repeatable workshop lab attached to Junior/Senior Capstone or Topic Studios.
  • Function: Brief, targeted deep-dives into rapidly evolving tools (e.g., advanced variable fonts, WebGL/3D UI, local AI integration, modern dev handoff) taken alongside 3000/4000-level project work.

Option B: Embedded Upper-Level Touchpoints

  • Junior Year (Systems & Interaction): Reiterate DTII 2760 Unit 2 & 4 principles by requiring live, tokenized design systems and responsive component libraries within Branding and UI/UX studios.
  • Senior Year (Capstone & Professional Practice): Reiterate DTI 2750 Unit 1 & DTII 2760 Unit 3 through mandatory pre-flight production audits, digital asset archiving, portfolio performance optimization, and interactive prototype presentations.

Position & Framework: Design Technology Sequence

Purpose

Design Technology I and Design Technology II provide the sophomore-level technological foundation for contemporary graphic design practice.

While software skills remain important, the sequence positions technology not as a collection of tools, but as a design medium through which information is structured, translated, produced, and experienced across media.

Students investigate how technologies — including materials, standards, tools, workflows, systems, and emerging computational processes — shape design decisions and influence communication.

The sequence prepares students to work across print, screen, interaction, and emerging technologies while developing durable habits of systems thinking, production literacy, research, creative experimentation, and professional workflow.

Position Statement

Design Technology is the study of how information is structured, translated, produced, and made responsive across media.

Contemporary designers work within technological systems regardless of specialization. Whether designing publications, interfaces, products, environments, motion graphics, or emerging media experiences, designers must understand how information behaves across platforms, formats, audiences, and contexts.

Technology is understood broadly to include:

  • material systems
  • production systems
  • information systems
  • communication systems
  • computational systems

Examples include:

  • paper and print technologies
  • typography and grid systems
  • color and reproduction systems
  • file and workflow systems
  • web standards
  • component libraries
  • design systems
  • AI-assisted workflows

Students learn that technologies are not neutral. Every technology contains assumptions, defaults, possibilities, and constraints that influence design outcomes.

The purpose of Design Technology is therefore not software mastery for its own sake. The purpose is to develop designers who can:

  • understand media and production constraints
  • translate information across formats and contexts
  • build structured and scalable systems
  • design interactive and responsive experiences
  • critically engage emerging technologies
  • adapt to future tools and workflows

Technology becomes a vehicle for understanding design rather than an end in itself.

Relationship to Department Pillars

Pillar Design Technology Contribution
Cognition Understanding design through technology, systems, media, and production environments
Creative Confidence Experimentation, prototyping, iteration, and exploration across media
Research Observation, testing, evaluation, and evidence-based design decisions
Tools Technical fluency with contemporary design workflows and production environments
Future-Focused Professional Organization, collaboration, documentation, handoff, and adaptable learning practices
Advocacy Accessibility, ethics, sustainability, copyright, licensing, and responsible technology use

Rather than existing separately from the departmental framework, Design Technology provides a practical environment through which each pillar becomes visible and actionable.

Cognitive Framework

Design Technology investigates how information is structured, organized, translated, produced, and experienced across media.

Students learn to analyze:

  • structure
  • hierarchy
  • systems
  • interaction
  • behavior
  • production

through the lens of contemporary technology.

Technology is understood not simply as software, but as the environment through which design is created, distributed, reproduced, and experienced.

Sequence Philosophy

The sophomore sequence progresses from understanding media and production toward understanding systems and behavior.

Students move from creating individual outputs toward designing adaptable systems capable of operating across platforms, audiences, and contexts.

Design Technology I Design Technology II
Media Systems
Translation Interaction
Output Behavior
Assets Components
Structure Responsiveness

This progression establishes a foundation for advanced coursework in interaction design, motion design, emerging media, design systems, professional practice, and future technologies.

Sophomore Design Technology Lens

Across both semesters, students repeatedly engage five core questions:

Question Focus
Structure How is information organized?
Translation How does information change across media?
System What rules create consistency and scalability?
Behavior How does information respond to users, context, or time?
Defaults What assumptions are built into the technology?

These questions provide continuity across projects, tools, and technological environments.

The concept of defaults encourages students to recognize that every technology contains embedded decisions.

Examples may include:

  • paper sizes
  • browser defaults
  • operating-system conventions
  • typographic conventions
  • templates
  • accessibility settings
  • AI-generated outputs

Students learn to evaluate, challenge, and intentionally work with these defaults.

Design Technology I

Media + Translation + Output

Course Description

Design Technology I introduces students to the technological foundations of contemporary design practice.

Students develop fluency with digital media, production workflows, structured information, and design translation across print, screen, and web environments.

The course emphasizes media literacy, organization, workflow, production, and material understanding while introducing systems thinking through typography, layout, publication design, and structured web media.

Core Questions

  • How does design change across media?
  • How do production constraints influence design decisions?
  • How is information structured and organized?
  • How do workflows support effective design practice?
  • How do technologies shape communication?
  • What assumptions are built into the tools and systems we use?

Student Outcome

Students become capable of creating, organizing, translating, and producing design across multiple media while understanding the systems that support production.

Design Technology II

Systems + Interaction + Behavior

Course Description

Design Technology II expands foundational technological literacy into systems thinking, interaction, responsiveness, and behavior.

Students move beyond individual artifacts toward designing adaptable systems that respond to users, content, context, and time.

The course emphasizes interaction design, design systems, prototyping, motion, responsive environments, and emerging technologies.

Core Questions

  • How do people interact with information?
  • How do systems create consistency and adaptability?
  • How does design behave over time?
  • How do technologies shape user experience?
  • How can systems evolve across contexts?
  • How do emerging technologies influence design practice?

Student Outcome

Students become capable of designing interactive, responsive, and scalable systems that support contemporary communication across media.

Semester Structure

Design Technology I

Unit 1 — Digital Foundations

Focus

Understanding the digital environment as a design environment.

Topics

  • operating systems
  • file organization
  • metadata
  • cloud and local storage
  • asset management
  • fonts and licensing
  • file formats
  • raster and vector media
  • workflow fundamentals
  • information organization
  • naming and versioning systems

Project Direction

Create and manage a personal design asset system.

Unit 2 — Media, Materials, and Translation

Focus

Understanding how visual information changes across media.

Topics

  • image editing
  • vector construction
  • asset preparation
  • format conversion
  • color systems
  • color spaces
  • reproduction technologies
  • paper systems
  • substrates
  • ink and print technologies
  • fidelity and reproduction
  • media constraints
  • adaptation across formats

Project Direction

Translate a visual concept across multiple media outputs while evaluating how material and technological constraints affect communication.

Unit 3 — Publication and Information Systems

Focus

Structure, hierarchy, and communication through layout systems.

Topics

  • typographic systems
  • hierarchy systems
  • modular scales
  • grids
  • information architecture
  • content organization
  • content hierarchy
  • publication workflows
  • print production

Project Direction

Design a publication system that organizes complex information across multiple pages and formats.

Unit 4 — Structured Screen Media

Focus

Design as structure rather than appearance.

Topics

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • semantic structure
  • accessibility
  • responsive layouts
  • content-first design
  • web standards
  • screen-based production
  • responsive typography

Project Direction

Translate a publication system into a responsive screen-based experience.

Design Technology II

Unit 1 — Interaction Foundations

Focus

Designing information for use and navigation.

Topics

  • information architecture
  • user journeys
  • user research
  • task analysis
  • wireframes
  • prototyping
  • usability evaluation

Project Direction

Design an interactive information experience.

Unit 2 — Components and Design Systems

Focus

Moving from assets toward reusable systems.

Topics

  • assets versus components
  • reusable patterns
  • components
  • variables
  • design tokens
  • documentation
  • governance
  • scalable systems

Project Direction

Build a component-based design system.

Unit 3 — Motion and Behavior

Focus

Communication through time, feedback, and interaction.

Topics

  • motion principles
  • transitions
  • animation
  • state changes
  • affordances
  • feedback systems
  • time-based communication

Project Direction

Design a motion-enhanced interactive experience.

Unit 4 — Responsive and Generative Systems

Focus

Design systems that adapt to context, content, and emerging technologies.

Topics

  • responsive systems
  • dynamic content
  • APIs
  • computational design
  • AI-assisted workflows
  • generative processes
  • adaptive experiences

Project Direction

Develop a responsive, generative, or adaptive design system.

Cross-Sequence Themes

The following themes are introduced, revisited, and expanded throughout both semesters.

Theme DT I DT II
Accessibility Structure and production Interaction and behavior
Research Evaluation and testing User-centered design
Creative Confidence Exploration and experimentation Prototyping and iteration
Systems Thinking Organization and structure Components and scalability
Professional Practice Workflow and production Collaboration and documentation
Emerging Technology Contemporary tools and AI literacy Generative and adaptive systems
Technology as Systems Materials, media, and standards Platforms, components, and behavior

These themes function as recurring lenses rather than isolated topics.

Sophomore Outcome

Upon completion of the sequence, students will be able to:

  • work fluently across print, screen, and web environments
  • understand material and digital production systems
  • organize and manage complex design assets
  • translate information across media
  • understand how technologies shape communication
  • create structured design systems
  • distinguish between assets and reusable components
  • prototype and evaluate interactive experiences
  • design responsive and scalable solutions
  • collaborate within professional workflows
  • critically engage emerging technologies
  • apply accessibility, ethics, and advocacy principles to design practice

The sequence establishes a foundation for advanced study while preparing students for a rapidly evolving technological landscape.

02 Design Technology I/01 Syllabus.html.content:
Course Syllabus: Design Technology I

Media + Translation + Output

Credits: 3

Format: Lecture + Lab

Meeting Schedule:

  • TUE: Lecture / Orchestrator (1 hr 10 min) — Cohort-wide instructional session focused on core concepts, systems thinking, design history/ethics, technical logic, and live methodology demonstrations.
  • THU: Lab / Breakout Orientator (50 min) — Immediate hands-on breakout lab focused on tactical application, software execution, live troubleshooting, peer critique, and guided project development.

Course Description

Design Technology I introduces students to the technological foundations of contemporary design practice through an integrated Lecture + Lab structure.

Tuesday lectures establish essential systems thinking, digital media theory, technical logic, and production workflows.

Thursday labs provide an intensive, guided studio environment where students directly apply lecture concepts through hands-on software execution, file preflighting, live troubleshooting, and iterative project development across print, screen, and web environments.

Core Questions

  • How does design change across media?
  • How do production constraints influence design decisions?
  • How is information structured and organized?
  • How do workflows support effective design practice?
  • How do technologies shape communication?
  • What assumptions are built into the tools and systems we use?

Student Outcome

Students become capable of creating, organizing, translating, and producing design across multiple media while understanding the systems that support production.

Course Structure: Lecture vs. Lab Cadence

  • TUE Lecture (Systems & Logic): Focuses on technical theory, file environments, color/resolution science, grid mechanics, workflow architecture, and critical discussions around design ethics, web accessibility, and artificial intelligence.
  • THU Lab (Execution & Troubleshooting): Focuses on tactical tool application (Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, VS Code), file directory construction, font installation, code execution, live bug fixing, and peer feedback.

Course Outcomes and Learning Objectives

Students who successfully complete this course will have demonstrated competency across the following areas, grounded in the framework for future-ready practice:

TOOLS

Course Outcome: Develop foundational computer and file fluency as the prerequisite infrastructure for all design work across the program.

  • Lecture Focus: Analyze the mathematical logic of raster vs. vector environments, resolution standards (300 dpi vs. 72 dpi+), CSS grid frameworks, and color specification systems.
  • Lab Focus: Apply tools in Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, and VS Code; navigate OS environments; execute font installation; and preflight/export files for production.

Objectives:

  • Apply raster, vector, and layout tools (Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign) at a foundational level.
  • Execute CSS grid implementation and fundamental HTML structuring.
  • Navigate the OS environment, establish file management structures, and execute font installation.
  • Distinguish between raster and vector environments and select the appropriate application for specific tasks.
  • Manage file formats effectively for applications, imagery, and typography.
  • Apply resolution standards appropriately for print (300 dpi) and digital output (72 dpi+).
  • Utilize correct color spaces (RGB, CMYK) and specification systems (Pantone, Hexadecimal).
  • Prepare, preflight, and export files for physical and digital production.

COGNITION

Course Outcome: Understand the digital environment as the conceptual foundation for all design work, treating files, formats, tools, and workflows as intentional design decisions.

  • Lecture Focus: Articulate the relationship between operating systems, storage environments, and the programmatic mechanics of typographic grids.
  • Lab Focus: Implement proper file format selection based on output media and build structured grid systems directly within software tools.

Objectives:

  • Articulate how operating systems, files, folders, applications, and storage environments relate.
  • Understand the conceptual and mathematical differences between raster and vector logic.
  • Select appropriate file formats based on media constraints and output contexts.
  • Recognize technology as an extension of visual design, not an isolated technical track.
  • Understand programmatic mechanics of typographic grids alongside their visual application.

CREATIVE CONFIDENCE

Course Outcome: Build comfort and technical fluency through design practice, cross-media translation, and active iteration.

  • Lecture Focus: Evaluate cross-media translation strategies, visual consistency across platforms, and workflow efficiency.
  • Lab Focus: Rapidly prototype visual concepts, experiment with toolsets during guided lab breakouts, and solve real-time software challenges.

Objectives:

  • Learn toolsets by solving applied design problems rather than isolated software tutorials.
  • Translate identical content systems across multiple media formats and technical environments.
  • Develop confidence in switching between distinct digital tools and production workflows.
  • Cultivate habits of rapid iteration and low-stakes experimentation in digital spaces.

RESEARCH

Course Outcome: Utilize technical knowledge and system constraints to make evidence-based production decisions.

  • Lecture Focus: Examine color space mechanics (RGB, CMYK, Pantone), substrate constraints, and sustainable digital asset optimization.
  • Lab Focus: Perform resolution testing, asset compression, color profile conversion checks, and substrate preparation in software.

Objectives:

  • Research and apply precise resolution, color, and format standards for specific output contexts.
  • Analyze the production implications of color space conversion and substrate selection.
  • Investigate sustainable digital production practices, including asset optimization and reducing digital weight.

FUTURE FOCUSED PROFESSIONAL

Course Outcome: Establish professional file management, organizational habits, and workflow conventions that scale into studio environments.

  • Lecture Focus: Study studio asset pipelines, version control logic, local vs. cloud storage architectures, and handoff protocols.
  • Lab Focus: Build uniform file naming conventions, construct local/cloud directory trees, and assemble handoff packages.

Objectives:

  • Implement consistent file naming, folder structuring, and version management systems.
  • Differentiate operational logic between local storage, networked environments, and cloud systems.
  • Develop organized handoff conventions for both print vendors and digital collaborators.

ADVOCACY

Course Outcome: Develop critical awareness of technology's embedded defaults, ethical implications, and accessibility requirements.

  • Lecture Focus: Discuss AI-assisted design ethics, copyright law, font licensing, and ecological impacts of digital media.
  • Lab Focus: Implement contrast accessibility checks, write WCAG-compliant semantic HTML, and verify font licensing in active project files.

Objectives:

  • Understand AI-assisted design capabilities, limitations, and current ethical considerations.
  • Navigate copyright, font licensing, and intellectual property within digital practice.
  • Apply foundational web accessibility standards, including semantic HTML and contrast requirements.
  • Recognize the ecological and material implications of both physical and digital production.

Course Materials & Technologies

  • Textbook: Graphic Design Rules: 365 Essential Design Dos and Don'ts (or equivalent foundational text)
  • OER Resources: Mozilla Developer Network (MDN) Web Docs for HTML/CSS standards
  • Reference: Manufacturer documentation for print standards and Adobe Creative Cloud workflows
  • Software: Adobe Creative Cloud (Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign), VS Code, Canvas LMS
  • Supplies: External solid-state drive (SSD) for local backups, sketchbook for wireframing and structural planning

Learning Activities & Assessments

  • Asset System Project (Lab Benchmark): Build a personal digital infrastructure, establishing system file-naming conventions and cloud/local backup structures. This ensures foundational OS and workflow literacy.
  • Cross-Media Translation Project (Lecture + Lab): Translate a single visual concept into an optimized print poster (CMYK/300 dpi) and screen graphic (RGB/72 dpi+). This assesses understanding of resolution, color space, and format conversion.
  • Publication System Design (Lecture + Lab): Structure multi-page complex text using master pages, paragraph styles, character styles, and baseline grids. This evaluates typographic systems thinking and layout software fluency.
  • Responsive Screen Build (Lab Focus): Translate publication assets into a semantic HTML/CSS web layout adhering to accessibility standards. This assesses understanding of structured information, CSS grids, and accessibility defaults.

Grade Distribution

Course Component Operational Model Total Points
Digital Foundations (Asset System) Lab-Driven Setup & Audit 150
Media Translation Project Lecture Theory + Lab Execution 250
Publication System Lecture Logic + Lab Execution 250
Structured Screen Media Lab-Driven Build 250
Professional Practice (Workflow, Lab Participation, & Organization) Ongoing Lecture & Lab 100
Total Points Possible 1000

Course Modules: Design Technology I

MO 1: Digital Foundations

Introduction

Welcome to Module 1. Before launching into complex visual design, you must master the environment in which you work. This module establishes your personal digital infrastructure. You will learn to treat file paths, cloud syncing, metadata, and folder structures not as administrative chores, but as intentional design decisions. This module culminates in the Asset System Project, where you will build and test a professional, scalable storage and backup framework that will support your entire design career.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 1.1: Navigate local, networked, and cloud OS environments to establish resilient file management and version control structures. (Future Focused Professional)
  • MLO 1.2: Install fonts, manage font licenses, and differentiate between application-specific and universal file formats. (Tools / Advocacy)
  • MLO 1.3: Articulate how data storage structures, metadata, and file naming conventions impact collaborative studio workflows. (Cognition)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Graphic Design Rules, Section: "File Management and Organization Basics" (or equivalent chapter on workflow).
  • Read: "Understanding File Formats: Native vs. Exchange Files" (Adobe Workflow Documentation).
  • Watch: Mastering the OS: Local Storage vs. Cloud Syncing Mechanics (Instructor Video Tutorial).

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 1:

  • TUE Lecture: System Architecture — OS logic, directory paths, file-naming protocols, and cloud vs. local storage models.
  • THU Lab: Local Infrastructure Setup — Building folder trees, establishing naming conventions, and configuring backup syncing.

Week 2:

  • TUE Lecture: Asset Integrity — Font licensing, copyright, metadata preservation, and catastrophe-proofing your workflow.
  • THU Lab: System Audit & Testing — Font installer navigation, SSD drive partition setup, and live peer directory reviews.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): "The Ethics of Typography: Font Licensing and Piracy in Modern Studio Practice."
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Asset System Setup: Submit a PDF manual and a live shared cloud directory link demonstrating your standardized folder structure and backup protocol.
  • Quiz: Digital Environment & File Format Literacy Quiz.

MO 2: Media, Materials, and Translation

Introduction

A design is never independent of its medium. In Module 2, you will discover how a single visual idea morphs when it moves between a glowing screen and a physical sheet of paper. Through the Cross-Media Translation Project, you will author a single visual concept and translate it into two distinct outputs: an optimized print poster and a screen-ready graphic. Along the way, you will wrestle directly with the math of resolution, the mechanics of color spaces, and the constraints of physical substrates.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 2.1: Execute fundamental raster operations in Photoshop and vector construction in Illustrator. (Tools)
  • MLO 2.2: Translate a single visual system across print and digital media, successfully calculating resolution differences (300dpi vs. 72dpi) and shifting between CMYK/Pantone and RGB/Hexadecimal color spaces. (Creative Confidence / Research)
  • MLO 2.3: Analyze the production implications of color space conversion, ink limits, and paper substrate selection on visual fidelity. (Research)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Graphic Design Rules, Rules: "Color Spaces (RGB vs. CMYK)" and "Resolution Realities."
  • Read: The Designer's Guide to Print Production & Substrates (Manufacturer Documentation).
  • Watch: How to Preflight, Package, and Export Clean Files for Commercial Print Vendors (Screencast).

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 3:

  • TUE Lecture: Vector vs. Raster Logic — Geometry vs. pixel arrays, software domain boundaries, and color space theory.
  • THU Lab: Vector Construction & Image Editing — Pen tool efficiency, raster manipulation, and color mode configuration in Illustrator/Photoshop.

Week 4:

  • TUE Lecture: The Math of Output — DPI/PPI formulas, effective resolution, screen refresh considerations, and file compression.
  • THU Lab: Media Translation Workbench — Resampling images, converting color profiles, and setting up bleed/crop boundaries.

Week 5:

  • TUE Lecture: Substrates & Sustainability — Paper weight, ink limits, digital weight optimization, and environmental impacts of production.
  • THU Lab: Preflight Lab & Vendor Handoff — Running preflight profiles, packaging files with linked assets, and generating production PDFs.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): "The Ecological Footprint of Media: Comparing the Environmental Impact of Print vs. High-Weight Digital Assets."
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Cross-Media Translation Deliverables: Submit an interactive PDF package containing a print-ready vector/raster poster file (packaged with links/fonts) alongside a web-optimized screen graphic asset.
  • Quiz: Vector vs. Raster Logic and Color Space Mechanics.

MO 3: Publication and Information Systems

Introduction

How do you guide a reader through thousands of words of text across dozens of pages? Module 3 introduces systems thinking through typography and layout architecture. You will shift your focus from single-page layouts to complex, multi-page documents. In the Publication System Design Project, you will use InDesign to tame complex text copy, establishing visual hierarchy using modular typographic scales, baseline grids, master pages, and automated text styles.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 3.1: Apply advanced layout software tools in InDesign, including master pages, paragraph styles, character styles, and automated text threading. (Tools)
  • MLO 3.2: Understand and implement the mathematical logic of typographic grids and modular scales alongside their aesthetic application. (Cognition)
  • MLO 3.3: Organize complex text copy into a highly scannable, logical information hierarchy across a multi-page publication layout. (Cognition / Creative Confidence)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Graphic Design Rules, Section: "The Grid: Breaking it, Making it" and "Typographic Hierarchy Dos and Don'ts."
  • Read: Adobe InDesign Documentation: "Working with Paragraph and Character Styles."
  • Watch: The Power of the Baseline: Aligning Multi-Column Typographic Layouts (Video Walkthrough).

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 6:

  • TUE Lecture: Typographic Systems & Grids — Baseline grid math, column structures, modular proportions, and typographic hierarchy.
  • THU Lab: Grid Construction — Document setup in InDesign, baseline grid mapping, and margins/column configuration.

Week 7:

  • TUE Lecture: Automation Mechanics — Style sheets, parent page inheritance, running headers, and multi-page layout logic.
  • THU Lab: Stylesheet Workshop — Creating nested paragraph/character styles, object styles, and master page templates.

Week 8:

  • TUE Lecture: Information Flow & Copyfitting — Managing complex long-form copy, widows/orphans, text threading, and prepress checks.
  • THU Lab: Multi-Page Production & Preflight — Threading long text, fine-tuning rag/hyphenation, and exporting print-ready publication packages.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): "Copyright, Creative Commons, and Intellectual Property Rights for Layout Designers."
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Multi-Page Publication System: Submit a multi-page, packaged InDesign layout demonstrating grid enforcement, parent page mapping, and clean paragraph/character style sheets.
  • Quiz: Typographic Math, Grids, and Software Hierarchy.

MO 4: Structured Screen Media

Introduction

In this final module, you will learn to view web design not as drawing pictures of web pages, but as building responsive, flexible information systems. In the Responsive Screen Build Project, you will translate the multi-page print publication system you designed in Module 3 into a functioning, responsive website. Using VS Code, you will write semantic HTML and CSS Grid layouts to ensure your text fluidly adapts to any screen size while remaining completely accessible to users with disabilities.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 4.1: Build semantic HTML structures and style them using CSS Grid and flexbox frameworks. (Tools)
  • MLO 4.2: Translate a static print typographic layout system into a dynamic, content-first, fluid screen environment. (Creative Confidence)
  • MLO 4.3: Integrate foundational web accessibility requirements (WCAG color contrast minimums, descriptive alt tags, and semantic structure) into custom web layouts. (Advocacy)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Mozilla Developer Network (MDN) Web Docs: "Getting Started with HTML" and "CSS Grid Layout."
  • Read: Introduction to Web Accessibility (W3C): "Understanding Semantic Markup and Contrast."
  • Watch: Responsive Typography: Building Fluid Text with CSS Viewport Units (Coding Tutorial).

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 9:

  • TUE Lecture: Print to Screen System Translation — Comparing static page bounds to fluid DOM trees, viewport mechanics, and text hierarchy.
  • THU Lab: VS Code & File Structure Setup — Setting up local web directories, root folders, relative file paths, and live-server environments.

Week 10:

  • TUE Lecture: Semantic Markup & Architecture — HTML structure, document object models (DOM), head/body relationships, and semantic tags.
  • THU Lab: Writing Semantic HTML — Translating publication text into <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <footer> elements.

Week 11:

  • TUE Lecture: CSS Foundations & The Box Model — Selectors, specificity, margins, padding, borders, and typography styling rules.
  • THU Lab: Styling Workshop — Linking external CSS files, defining typography properties, and managing box-model spacing.

Week 12:

  • TUE Lecture: Fluid Layouts & Grid Mechanics — CSS Grid, Flexbox, fractional units (fr), and media query logic.
  • THU Lab: Building CSS Grids — Writing fluid grid structures, flex containers, and mobile/desktop breakpoint shifts.

Week 13:

  • TUE Lecture: Inclusive Design & WCAG Standards — Accessibility principles, color contrast calculations, screen readers, and alt-text strategy.
  • THU Lab: Accessibility Auditing — Running accessibility checkers, resolving contrast errors, adding ARIA labels, and testing keyboard navigation.

Week 14:

  • TUE Lecture: AI in Code & Optimization — Front-end automation tools, asset weight optimization, clean code practices, and deployment pipelines.
  • THU Lab: Final Build Packaging — Optimizing web image assets, validating code syntax, and bundling the final deployment directory.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): "The Ethics of AI in Code and Design: Automation, Attribution, and the Future of the Front-End Environment."
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Responsive Web Build: Submit a working, multi-page front-end web directory (HTML, CSS, and optimized image assets) compressed into a clean deployment package.
  • Quiz: Semantic HTML, Basic CSS Syntax, and Accessibility Compliance.

Project 01: The Studio Infrastructure

Digital Foundations & Asset System

Canvas Assignment Settings:

  • Points: 150
  • Submission Type: Online
    File Upload + Text Entry
  • Allowed File Types: .pdf, .zip

Project Overview

Before we design, we build the studio. In the physical world, a designer needs a clean desk, organized flat files, and a system for finding their tools. In the digital environment, your operating system (OS), folder structures, and file naming conventions are your studio.

In this project, you will establish the foundational digital infrastructure you will use for the rest of the program. You are shifting from acting as a "student saving homework" to a "future-focused professional managing design assets."

Pillars Addressed: Cognition, Future-Focused Professional

Course Outcomes: Navigate the OS environment, establish file management structures, and implement a reliable cloud/local backup system.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this project, you will be able to:

  1. Design and implement a scalable folder hierarchy for your coursework.
  2. Establish a consistent, professional file-naming convention.
  3. Differentiate between local storage, networked environments, and cloud backups.
  4. Prevent catastrophic data loss through a redundancy strategy.

Lecture vs. Lab Execution Schedule

  • TUE Lecture Briefing: System logic overview, file-naming rules (no spaces, version control, ISO dates), local vs. cloud storage mechanics, and manual documentation standards.
  • THU Lab Execution: Guided setup of folder trees, SSD backup drive configuration, live cloud-sync verification, and instructor pre-flight check of directory links.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Part 1: The Naming Convention

(Lecture Logic / Lab Setup)

Design a standard file-naming convention that you will use for all design files moving forward. It must account for:

  • Project Name or Course Code
  • Version Control (e.g., v01, v02, FINAL)
  • Date (Standardized format like YYYYMMDD)
  • General Rule: No spaces, no special characters (use underscores or dashes)._

Part 2: The Folder Architecture

(Lab Execution)

Create a master folder structure on your local drive for the current academic year.

  • Organize by Semester -> Course -> Projects -> Working Files vs. Final Assets.
  • Create an "Asset Library" folder for global assets (fonts, stock images, textures) that you will use across multiple classes.

Part 3: The Backup Strategy

(Lab Execution)

Set up an automated cloud backup (e.g., Google Drive, Dropbox, or OneDrive) that mirrors your local working directory and connects to your external SSD.

Part 4: The Infrastructure Manual

(Lab Deliverable)

Create a 1-2 page PDF "Studio Manual" documenting your system. This serves as your personal rulebook.

  • Include the formula for your naming convention with three examples.
  • Include screenshots of your Finder/File Explorer showing your new, pristine folder architecture.
  • Include a screenshot showing your folders successfully synced to your cloud storage.

Submission Requirements

Please submit the following:

  1. Your Studio Manual (PDF): The 1-2 page document outlining your naming conventions and featuring your screenshots.
  2. Text Entry Reflection: In the Canvas submission comment box, write a brief paragraph (3-4 sentences) explaining why this strict system is necessary when working collaboratively on a design team.

Grading Rubric (150 Points)

Criteria Excellent (100%) Proficient (80%) Developing (60%) Needs Work (0-50%) Pts
Naming Convention Clear, logical, uses version control/dates, no spaces. System works but lacks one element (e.g., dates). Inconsistent rules or uses spaces/special characters. No clear system developed. 40
Folder Architecture Highly organized, scalable, clearly separates working/final assets. Functional structure but lacks deep organization. Disorganized or shallow structure. Folders are chaotic or missing. 40
Backup Proof Clear evidence (screenshots) of local-to-cloud syncing. Evidence provided, but sync status is unclear. Missing cloud or local proof. No evidence of backup. 40
Professional Reflection Insightful, addresses team collaboration and workflow. Good explanation, but surface-level. Vague understanding of why infrastructure matters. Reflection missing or off-topic. 30

Project 02: Cross-Media Translation

Media, Materials, & Translation

Canvas Assignment Settings:

  • Points: 200
  • Submission Type: Online
    File Upload
  • Allowed File Types: .pdf, .zip

Project Overview

Design does not exist independently of its medium. A visual system that succeeds on a glowing phone screen may completely fail when printed on paper, and a poster designed for a press may become illegible when compressed into a social media graphic. Professional designers must understand not only how to create visuals, but how those visuals change as they move between different methods of production.

In this project, you will develop a single visual concept and intentionally translate it across two distinct media: a professionally prepared print poster and a screen-optimized digital graphic. Rather than creating two unrelated designs, you will build one cohesive visual system that adapts to the unique technical, physical, and perceptual requirements of each environment.

Throughout the project you will make informed decisions about raster versus vector graphics, color spaces, image resolution, typography, file optimization, and production workflows. By the end, you will understand that successful design is not simply about aesthetics—it is about choosing the right technical solution for a given medium.

Pillars Addressed: Creative Confidence, Research, Tools

Course Outcomes: Execute raster and vector workflows, translate visual systems across print and digital environments, and prepare production-ready files for professional output.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this project, you will be able to:

  1. Develop a unified visual concept that functions across multiple media.
  2. Apply vector and raster workflows appropriately for different production needs.
  3. Prepare files using correct color spaces, image resolutions, and export settings.
  4. Produce professional-quality print-ready and screen-ready deliverables using industry-standard workflows.

Lecture vs. Lab Execution Schedule

  • TUE Lecture Briefing: Principles of media translation, raster versus vector graphics, RGB versus CMYK color spaces, image resolution, substrates, and production workflows.
  • THU Lab Execution: Illustrator and Photoshop workflow demonstrations, image editing, vector construction, color profile conversion, preflight checks, packaging assets, and export optimization.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Part 1: Develop a Visual System

(Lecture Logic / Lab Planning)

Begin by creating a single visual concept centered around a topic of your choice (or one provided by the instructor). Your concept should include:

  • A clear visual hierarchy
  • Consistent typography
  • A defined color palette
  • Supporting imagery or illustration
  • A unified visual style

This concept will serve as the foundation for every deliverable in the project.

Part 2: Print Translation

(Lab Execution)

Translate your concept into a print-ready poster suitable for commercial production.

Your poster should include:

  • Appropriate page dimensions
  • Bleed and safety margins
  • CMYK color mode
  • High-resolution imagery (300 ppi minimum)
  • Properly prepared vector graphics
  • Organized layers and linked assets

Before exporting, perform a complete preflight review to identify missing fonts, broken links, or production errors.

Part 3: Screen Translation

(Lab Execution)

Adapt the same visual system into a digital graphic optimized for screen viewing.

Your digital version should demonstrate:

  • RGB color space
  • Appropriate pixel dimensions
  • Optimized file size
  • Legible typography on screen
  • Appropriate image compression
  • Export settings suited for digital distribution

Rather than simply resizing the poster, thoughtfully redesign the composition to accommodate the constraints and opportunities of digital media.

Part 4: Production Package

(Lab Deliverable)

Prepare a professional production package containing all project assets.

Your package should include:

  • Packaged Illustrator and/or Photoshop working files
  • Linked images
  • Required fonts (where licensing permits)
  • Print-ready PDF
  • Screen-ready PNG or JPG
  • A short production summary describing the technical decisions you made during translation

Submission Requirements

Please submit the following:

  1. Compressed Project Folder (.zip) containing:
    • Native Illustrator and/or Photoshop files
    • Packaged assets
    • Print-ready PDF
    • Screen-ready image
  2. Production Summary (PDF):
    A one-page document explaining:
    • Why different color spaces were used
    • How image resolution changed between outputs
    • Any design modifications required during translation
    • Challenges encountered and how they were resolved

Grading Rubric (200 Points)

Criteria Excellent (100%) Proficient (80%) Developing (60%) Needs Work (0–50%) Pts
Visual System Cohesive concept successfully maintained across both media. Mostly consistent with minor inconsistencies. Visual system lacks cohesion between outputs. Two unrelated or incomplete designs. 50
Technical Translation Correct use of color spaces, resolution, raster/vector workflows, and export settings. Minor technical mistakes that do not significantly impact output. Multiple technical issues affecting quality. Incorrect workflows or missing production requirements. 60
Production Package Files are fully organized, packaged correctly, and production-ready. Mostly complete with minor organizational issues. Missing assets or incomplete packaging. Files cannot be opened or reproduced reliably. 50
Production Summary Demonstrates thoughtful analysis of technical decisions and media translation. Good explanation with limited technical depth. Reflection is brief or partially incomplete. Missing or unrelated documentation. 40

Project 03: Publication Systems

Publication & Information Systems

Canvas Assignment Settings:

  • Points: 250
  • Submission Type: Online
    File Upload
  • Allowed File Types: .pdf, .zip

Project Overview

Designing a single page is one challenge. Designing dozens of pages that remain clear, consistent, and easy to navigate is another entirely. Professional publications rely on systems—not individual decisions—to organize information. Grids, typographic scales, paragraph styles, parent pages, and document architecture allow designers to maintain consistency while managing large amounts of content efficiently.

In this project, you will transform an existing body of text into a professionally designed multi-page publication using Adobe InDesign. Rather than focusing on illustration or expressive composition, your primary objective is to create a structured information system that guides readers through complex content with clarity and consistency.

Throughout the project, you will develop a modular layout using baseline grids, columns, reusable styles, and automated document features. You will discover that thoughtful systems reduce repetitive work, improve readability, and allow large publications to evolve without sacrificing visual cohesion.

By the end of this project, you will understand that publication design is less about decorating pages and more about building repeatable frameworks that organize information at scale.

Pillars Addressed: Cognition, Creative Confidence, Tools

Course Outcomes: Apply advanced InDesign workflows, organize complex information through typographic systems, and produce professionally packaged multi-page publications.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this project, you will be able to:

  1. Design a modular publication system using grids and typographic hierarchy.
  2. Apply paragraph styles, character styles, object styles, and parent pages to automate document consistency.
  3. Organize long-form content into a clear, readable information hierarchy.
  4. Prepare a production-ready publication package suitable for professional printing or distribution.

Lecture vs. Lab Execution Schedule

  • TUE Lecture Briefing: Typographic hierarchy, modular grids, baseline grids, document architecture, parent pages, style automation, and long-form publication workflows.
  • THU Lab Execution: InDesign document setup, grid construction, stylesheet creation, threaded text, copyfitting, preflight review, packaging, and PDF export.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Part 1: Build the Publication Framework

(Lecture Logic / Lab Planning)

Begin by establishing the structural foundation of your publication before placing any content.

Your publication framework should include:

  • Document size and margins
  • Multi-column grid system
  • Baseline grid
  • Master (Parent) pages
  • Running headers and/or page numbering
  • Preliminary typographic scale

Think of this framework as the blueprint that every page will follow.

Part 2: Construct the Typographic System

(Lab Execution)

Develop a complete typographic hierarchy that will organize every level of information throughout the publication.

Create styles for:

  • Primary headings
  • Secondary headings
  • Body copy
  • Captions
  • Pull quotes or callouts
  • Lists and supporting text

Use Paragraph Styles, Character Styles, and Object Styles wherever appropriate instead of manually formatting text.

Part 3: Build the Publication

(Lab Execution)

Import the provided text (or instructor-approved content) into your document and organize it into a polished multi-page publication.

Your publication should demonstrate:

  • Threaded text across multiple pages
  • Consistent spacing and alignment
  • Effective hierarchy
  • Balanced typography
  • Proper handling of widows, orphans, and overset text
  • Consistent visual rhythm throughout the document

Images, graphics, and supporting elements should reinforce—not compete with—the information hierarchy.

Part 4: Production Package

(Lab Deliverable)

Prepare your publication for professional production.

Your submission package should include:

  • Native InDesign (.indd) file
  • Packaged document with linked assets
  • Fonts (when licensing permits)
  • Print-ready PDF
  • A one-page design rationale describing your layout system and workflow decisions

Before submitting, perform a complete preflight review to ensure there are no missing links, missing fonts, overset text, or export errors.

Submission Requirements

Please submit the following:

  1. Compressed Project Folder (.zip) containing:
    • Native InDesign document
    • Packaged project folder
    • Linked assets
    • Print-ready PDF
  2. Publication Design Summary (PDF):
    A one-page document explaining:
    • Your grid structure and layout decisions
    • How paragraph and character styles improved workflow
    • Challenges encountered while organizing large amounts of information
    • How your publication system could scale to additional pages

Grading Rubric (250 Points)

Criteria Excellent (100%) Proficient (80%) Developing (60%) Needs Work (0–50%) Pts
Publication System Strong modular grid, consistent hierarchy, and cohesive layout across all pages. Mostly consistent with minor layout inconsistencies. Grid or hierarchy is inconsistently applied. Publication lacks an organized structural system. 70
Typography & Automation Effective use of paragraph styles, character styles, object styles, parent pages, and text threading throughout. Most automation features are used correctly with minor inconsistencies. Limited use of styles or automation; manual formatting dominates. Styles and automation are largely absent or misused. 70
Technical Production Packaged correctly with clean links, no overset text, successful preflight, and professional export. Minor technical issues that do not affect usability. Several production issues requiring correction. Missing assets, broken links, or incomplete package. 60
Publication Design Summary Thoughtful explanation demonstrating understanding of systems thinking and publication workflow. Good explanation with adequate technical discussion. Reflection is brief or lacks technical insight. Missing or unrelated documentation. 50

03 Design Technology II/01 Syllabus.html.content:
Course Syllabus: Design Technology II

Systems + Interaction + Behavior

Credits: 3

Format: Lecture + Lab

Meeting Schedule:

  • TUE: Lecture / Orchestrator (1 hr 10 min) — Cohort-wide instructional session focused on interaction logic, systemic frameworks, design ethics, behavior theory, and live technology demonstrations.
  • THU: Lab / Breakout Orientator (50 min) — Immediate hands-on breakout lab focused on component construction, prototyping, Figma variable workflows, micro-interaction tuning, and guided project execution.

Course Description

Design Technology II expands foundational technological literacy into systems thinking, interaction design, responsiveness, and behavior through an integrated Lecture + Lab model.

Tuesday lectures establish the theoretical, cognitive, and ethical foundations of interaction—examining atomic design methodologies, usability heuristics, dynamic data logic, and generative AI implications.

Thursday labs provide an intensive, guided environment where students build reusable design systems, program interactive variables, prototype motion behaviors, and construct responsive interfaces across modern software environments.

Core Questions

  • How do people interact with information?
  • How do systems create consistency and adaptability?
  • How does design behave over time?
  • How do technologies shape user experience?
  • How can systems evolve across contexts?
  • How do emerging technologies influence design practice?

Student Outcome

Students become capable of designing interactive, responsive, and scalable systems that support contemporary communication across media while mastering component-driven tools in lab and systemic thinking in lecture.

Course Structure: Lecture vs. Lab Cadence

  • TUE Lecture (Systems & Behavior): Focuses on interaction paradigms, information architecture theory, design tokens, component architecture logic, motion choreography, and critical assessments of AI bias and WCAG web accessibility.
  • THU Lab (Execution & Prototyping): Focuses on technical execution in Figma and prototyping environments—constructing component libraries, mapping variables, setting up Smart Animate transitions, building responsive auto-layouts, and conducting usability tests.

Course Outcomes and Learning Objectives

Students who successfully complete this course will have demonstrated competency across the following areas, grounded in the framework for future-ready practice:

TOOLS

Course Outcome: Develop fluency in interaction design software, prototyping environments, and component-based workflows to build responsive systems.

  • Lecture Focus: Analyze the architecture of component-based design systems, variable scoping logic, timeline motion mechanics, and dynamic API integrations.
  • Lab Focus: Build Figma component libraries, program global variables/tokens, execute state-based animations, and construct auto-layouts with multi-breakpoint responsiveness.

Objectives:

  • Utilize industry-standard prototyping tools (e.g., Figma) to design screen-based experiences.
  • Construct and manage component libraries, global variables, and design tokens.
  • Execute temporal and state-based animations using timeline or interaction tools.
  • Integrate APIs, dynamic content, or generative AI workflows into design mockups.
  • Implement responsive layouts that adapt fluidly across multiple breakpoints.

COGNITION

Course Outcome: Expand structural thinking into systemic and behavioral thinking, designing rules rather than singular artifacts.

  • Lecture Focus: Study user journey mapping, task analysis frameworks, information architecture, and the logic of state changes over time.
  • Lab Focus: Translate user flows into low-fidelity structural wireframes, configure nested component variants, and map dynamic state interactions.

Objectives:

  • Distinguish between static design assets and reusable, scalable design components.
  • Analyze user journeys, task flows, and the information architecture of complex systems.
  • Understand the programmatic logic of variables, nested components, and state changes.
  • Anticipate how information behaves over time and responds to context or device changes.

CREATIVE CONFIDENCE

Course Outcome: Embrace the unpredictability of interactive and generative media through rapid prototyping and user testing.

  • Lecture Focus: Evaluate feedback loops, affordances, motion mechanics, and human-AI collaborative workflows.
  • Lab Focus: Prototype interactive state transitions, conduct rapid usability tests, iterate based on user feedback, and test generative prompt integrations.

Objectives:

  • Prototype interactive experiences quickly to test functional hypotheses.
  • Adapt design systems gracefully when introduced to unexpected user behavior or dynamic content.
  • Experiment with motion, feedback loops, and temporal transitions as core communication tools.
  • Navigate emerging technologies and AI generation as collaborative, rather than prescriptive, design tools.

RESEARCH

Course Outcome: Base interaction and system decisions on user observation, usability heuristics, and testing data.

  • Lecture Focus: Analyze usability heuristics (Nielsen Norman Group), task analysis methodologies, and motion affordance principles.
  • Lab Focus: Conduct user testing on interactive prototypes, track task success metrics, and audit motion effectiveness.

Objectives:

  • Conduct foundational user research, task analysis, and journey mapping.
  • Perform usability testing on prototypes and iterate based on actionable feedback.
  • Evaluate the effectiveness of motion and affordances in guiding user behavior.

FUTURE FOCUSED PROFESSIONAL

Course Outcome: Master the documentation, governance, and collaborative handoff processes required for modern digital product teams.

  • Lecture Focus: Study design system governance models, tokenization naming conventions, developer handoff standards, and version control.
  • Lab Focus: Author Figma Dev Mode specifications, create token handoff sheets, and manage shared component library updates.

Objectives:

  • Document design systems comprehensively for developer and cross-functional handoff.
  • Manage component versioning and library updates within a collaborative team environment.
  • Articulate interactive behaviors and logic clearly using professional terminology.

ADVOCACY

Course Outcome: Champion inclusive design, prioritize digital accessibility, and critically assess the societal impact of systemic technology choices.

  • Lecture Focus: Critique algorithmic bias in generative models, discuss user privacy ethics (Ruined by Design), and evaluate WCAG accessibility standards.
  • Lab Focus: Perform contrast calculations on design tokens, build screen-reader accessible wireframe structures, and test graceful degradation patterns.

Objectives:

  • Implement advanced web accessibility standards (WCAG guidelines, screen reader compatibility).
  • Evaluate generative systems and AI models for inherent biases or exclusionary defaults.
  • Design systems that degrade gracefully for users with low bandwidth or older devices.
  • Advocate for user privacy, ethical data patterns, and transparent systemic behavior.

Course Materials & Technologies

  • Textbook: Ruined by Design by Mike Monteiro (for ethical/advocacy context) or Atomic Design by Brad Frost (for systems context)
  • OER Resources: WCAG Accessibility Guidelines, Nielsen Norman Group articles on UX heuristics
  • Core Software: Figma (including Dev Mode, Auto-Layout, Variables, and Prototyping)
  • Motion & Behavior Tools: Figma Smart Animate, Principle, or After Effects
  • Emerging Tech: Generative AI tools (e.g., Midjourney, ChatGPT) and mock API endpoints
  • Reference: Figma community documentation, material design guidelines

Learning Activities & Assessments

  • Information Architecture & Wireframing (Lab Benchmark): Map a user journey and create structural wireframes for a complex digital task. This assesses research, task analysis, and cognitive organization.

  • Generative/Responsive Environment (Lab Focus): Design a system that adapts its content or layout based on varying data inputs, user contexts, or generative prompts. This evaluates adaptability and emerging technology literacy.

Course Modules: Design Technology II

MO 1: Interaction Foundations

Introduction

Welcome to Module 1. This module expands your foundational design literacy into interaction design and information architecture. Instead of focusing solely on how an interface looks, you will explore how it works and how people navigate information. You will learn to map out user journeys, conduct foundational research, and create structural wireframes for a complex digital task, culminating in an interactive information experience.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 1.1: Conduct foundational user research, task analysis, and journey mapping to understand user behavior. (Research)
  • MLO 1.2: Analyze user journeys, task flows, and the information architecture of complex systems to structure digital experiences. (Cognition)
  • MLO 1.3: Utilize industry-standard prototyping tools to design and wireframe screen-based experiences. (Tools)
  • MLO 1.4: Perform usability testing on prototypes and iterate based on actionable feedback. (Research)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Atomic Design by Brad Frost – Chapter 1: Designing Systems
  • Read: Nielsen Norman Group: Introduction to Information Architecture and UX Heuristics Workbook
  • Watch: Figma Tutorials: Getting Started with Wireframing and Prototyping Basics

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 1:

  • TUE Lecture: Interaction Logic — Task analysis, friction identification, and cognitive mapping.
  • THU Lab: Journey Mapping Workbench — Building user flows and task diagrams in FigJam.

Week 2:

  • TUE Lecture: Information Architecture — Tree testing, sitemaps, and mental models.
  • THU Lab: Wireframe Architecture — Setting up low-fidelity Figma canvases and frame grids.

Week 3:

  • TUE Lecture: Structural Hierarchy — Grayscale constraints, reading order, and affordances.
  • THU Lab: Grayscale Production — Building 5–7 core task wireframes without visual styling.

Week 4:

  • TUE Lecture: Usability & Feedback — Conducting usability tests and analyzing feedback loops.
  • THU Lab: Prototype Testing — Linking wireframes into clickable flows and running peer audits.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): Critique an existing application's user flow. Identify a point of friction and sketch an alternative solution.
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Project 1 Process Book: Submit user journey maps, IA diagrams, and low-fidelity Figma wireframe links.
  • Quiz: UX Usability Heuristics and Task Analysis Basics.

MO 2: Components and Design Systems

Introduction

In Module 2, we shift our focus from creating individual design assets to building reusable, scalable rules and components. You will master the technical logic of modern UI design by building a robust component library. This module introduces you to atomic design principles, auto-layout, global variables, and design tokens, challenging you to think like a system designer rather than a static visual artist.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 2.1: Distinguish between static design assets and reusable, scalable design components. (Cognition)
  • MLO 2.2: Construct and manage component libraries, global variables, and design tokens within Figma. (Tools)
  • MLO 2.3: Document design systems comprehensively for developer and cross-functional handoff, maintaining clear governance. (Future-Focused Professional)
  • MLO 2.4: Implement advanced web accessibility standards (WCAG guidelines) into design tokens and components. (Advocacy)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Atomic Design by Brad Frost – Chapters 2 & 3: The Atomic Design Methodology and The Design System Life Cycle
  • Read: Material Design Guidelines: Understanding Design Tokens
  • Watch: Figma Community: Deep Dive into Advanced Components, Auto-Layout, and Variables

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 5:

  • TUE Lecture: Atomic Systems — Atoms, molecules, organisms, and component breakdown theory.
  • THU Lab: Auto-Layout Workshop — Mastering padding, gap constraints, and responsive resizing.

Week 6:

  • TUE Lecture: Tokenization — Global vs. alias tokens, naming conventions, and dark mode mechanics.

  • THU Lab: Variable Programming — Setting up color, typography, and spacing variables in Figma.

Week 7:

  • TUE Lecture: Component States — Variant properties, component sets, and Boolean toggles.
  • THU Lab: Interactive UI Kit Build — Constructing nested buttons, inputs, and card components.

Week 8:

  • TUE Lecture: System Governance — Library updates, cross-functional communication, and Dev Mode logic.
  • THU Lab: Handoff Documentation — Building component specification sheets and developer guidelines.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): Tokenization Exercise. Share your strategy for naming global color and typography variables for light and dark modes.
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Project 2 Deliverables: Submit your organized Figma library featuring nested components, variants, design tokens, and a handoff sheet.

MO 3: Motion and Behavior

Introduction

Design doesn't sit still. Module 3 introduces time, transitions, and state changes as core communicative tools. You will explore motion principles to discover how subtle interface reactions act as "affordances" and feedback loops that guide human behavior. By animating micro-interactions and transitions, you will learn to manage user expectations across states and time.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 3.1: Execute temporal and state-based animations using timeline or interaction tools. (Tools)
  • MLO 3.2: Understand the programmatic logic of nested components and interactive state changes. (Cognition)
  • MLO 3.3: Experiment with motion, feedback loops, and temporal transitions as core communication tools. (Creative Confidence)
  • MLO 3.4: Evaluate the effectiveness of motion and affordances in guiding user behavior clearly and professionally. (Research / Professional)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Nielsen Norman Group: The Role of Animation in UX Design
  • Read: Material Design Guidelines: Motion Principles and Choreography
  • Watch: Figma / Principle Video Guide: Mastering Smart Animate, Micro-interactions, and Component States

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 9:

  • TUE Lecture: Motion Theory — Easing functions, duration standards, and functional vs. decorative motion.
  • THU Lab: Smart Animate Setup — Building basic hover states, toggles, and modal transitions.

Week 10:

  • TUE Lecture: Micro-Interactions — Trigger-rule-feedback loops and managing user expectations.
  • THU Lab: Interactive State Lab — Animating form validations, loading states, and inline feedback.

Week 11:

  • TUE Lecture: System Choreography — Multi-screen transitions, shared element transitions, and spatial continuity.
  • THU Lab: Prototype Construction — Connecting component states across multi-screen application flows.

Week 12:

  • TUE Lecture: Motion Evaluation — Auditing motion accessibility (reduced motion settings) and usability.
  • THU Lab: Recording & Export — Recording high-resolution prototype walkthroughs and exporting motion specs.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): Upload a screen recording of an effective micro-interaction from an app you use daily and write a brief analysis of its feedback mechanics.
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Project 3 Prototype: Submit an interactive prototype showcasing micro-interactions, complex state transitions, and a video walkthrough demonstrating system choreography.

MO 4: Responsive and Generative Systems

Introduction

The final module addresses the beautiful unpredictability of modern digital environments. Devices change, screen sizes shift, data is dynamic, and artificial intelligence is reshaping how content is generated. In Module 4, you will design fluid, responsive ecosystems that gracefully handle varying data inputs, API integrations, and AI workflows while championing accessibility and ethical data patterns.

Module Learning Objectives (MLOs)

Upon completion of this module, you should be able to:

  • MLO 4.1: Implement responsive layouts that adapt fluidly across multiple breakpoints. (Tools)
  • MLO 4.2: Integrate APIs, dynamic content, or generative AI workflows into design mockups and design systems. (Tools / Creative Confidence)
  • MLO 4.3: Design systems that degrade gracefully for users with low bandwidth or older devices. (Advocacy)
  • MLO 4.4: Evaluate generative systems and AI models for inherent biases or exclusionary defaults while advocating for ethical data patterns. (Advocacy)

Readings & Resources

  • Read: Ruined by Design by Mike Monteiro (Selected Chapters on design ethics, data privacy, and advocacy)
  • Read: W3C: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) Overview
  • Watch: Design Lecture Series: Designing with Dynamic Data, APIs, and Generative Artificial Intelligence

Weekly Lecture & Lab Breakdown

Week 13:

  • TUE Lecture: Fluid Screen Systems — Responsive layout rules, container constraints, and breakpoint architecture.
  • THU Lab: Multi-Breakpoint Workbench — Building adaptive frames using auto-layout wrap and fill rules.

Week 14:

  • TUE Lecture: Dynamic Content & AI — Designing for dynamic inputs, API data streams, and generative interface states.
  • THU Lab: Dynamic Data Integration — Populating Figma components with live JSON/API data plugins.

Week 15:

  • TUE Lecture: Ethical System Advocacy — Dark patterns, privacy considerations, and designing for low bandwidth.
  • THU Lab: Accessibility Audit & Final Handoff — Running WCAG color contrast checkers and finalizing documentation.

Activities & Assessments

  • Discussion (TUE Lecture Reflection): Ethical Tech Case Study. Analyze a modern AI platform or dynamic application regarding privacy and bias using Monteiro's text.
  • Assignment (THU Lab Deliverable): Project 4 Presentation: Submit a multi-breakpoint responsive prototype powered by dynamic content/mock APIs, alongside a 2-page design essay auditing accessibility and ethical patterns.
  • Quiz: Comprehensive Exam (WCAG guidelines, design system governance, and responsive principles).

03 Design Technology II/05 Project 01.ht.content:
Project 01: The Task Journey

Information Architecture & Interactive Wireframing

Canvas Assignment Settings:

  • Points: 200
  • Submission Type: Online
    Website URL / Figma Link + File Upload
  • Allowed File Types: .pdf (for Journey Map/IA)

Project Overview

Design Technology II moves us from designing artifacts to designing behaviors. Before we build interactive, high-fidelity design systems, we must understand how users navigate information to accomplish tasks.

For this project, introduced in Tuesday Lecture and engineered during Thursday Labs, you will act as an Interaction Designer tasked with restructuring a complex digital process. You will strip away visual styling (colors, typography, images) to focus purely on Information Architecture (IA), user flows, and structural wireframes.

Pillars Addressed: Cognition, Research, Systems

Course Outcomes: Map user journeys, analyze tasks, and utilize prototyping environments (Figma) to design structural wireframes.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this project, you will be able to:

  1. Conduct task analysis to break down a complex user goal into actionable steps.
  2. Map a User Journey that anticipates friction points and user contexts.
  3. Develop an Information Architecture (IA) map.
  4. Translate cognitive structure into low-fidelity, screen-based wireframes.

Lecture vs. Lab Execution Schedule

  • TUE Lecture Briefing: Usability heuristic theory, task analysis methodologies, friction point identification, grayscale constraint rules, and cognitive hierarchy.
  • THU Lab Execution: Guided user journey mapping in FigJam, information architecture diagramming, Figma frame setup, and peer usability testing of wireframe flows.

Step-by-Step Instructions

The Scenario

Choose one of the following notoriously complex digital tasks to restructure and improve:

  • Option A: Registering for classes on a university portal.
  • Option B: Booking a multi-city train or flight itinerary.
  • Option C: Checking out at an online grocery store with dietary-restricted substitutions.

Part 1: Task Analysis & User Journey

(Lecture Theory / Lab Mapping)

Break down the user's goal. Document their starting point, the steps they must take, the decisions they must make, and their endpoint. Map this out visually (using FigJam, Miro, or Illustrator) to show the "happy path" and potential points of friction.

Part 2: Information Architecture (IA)

(Lab Execution)

Create a site map / flow diagram showing the hierarchy of screens and information the user will encounter. How are the menus organized? What information lives on which screen?

Part 3: Low-Fidelity Wireframes

(Lab Execution)

Using Figma, translate your IA into low-fidelity structural wireframes.

  • Constraints: Use only shades of gray, one standard sans-serif font (Inter or Roboto), and placeholder boxes.
  • Strict Rule: No photos, logos, or branded colors. Focus entirely on hierarchy, scale, buttons, and reading order.
  • Design the core 5 to 7 screens required to complete the task you analyzed in Part 1.

Submission Requirements

Please submit the following:

  1. Journey & IA Document (PDF): A combined document containing your visual User Journey Map and Information Architecture diagram.
  2. Figma Link (URL): A link to your Figma file containing your low-fidelity wireframes. (Crucial: Ensure link sharing is set to "Anyone with the link can view").

Grading Rubric (200 Points)

Criteria Excellent (100%) Proficient (80%) Developing (60%) Needs Work (0-50%) Pts
Task Analysis & Journey Deep understanding of user steps, decisions, and friction points. Highly visual. Covers the basic steps but lacks deep insight into user friction. Misses key steps or decisions in the task process. Vague or incomplete journey mapping. 50
Information Architecture Clear, logical hierarchy. Screen structures make perfect cognitive sense. Functional IA, but some structural choices are confusing. Disorganized IA; information is grouped illogically. Missing or incomprehensible IA. 50
Wireframe Structure Excellent layout, hierarchy, and scale. Guides the eye perfectly through the task. Good layout, but some elements lack clear hierarchy or scaling. Poor use of scale, cluttered layout, or confusing navigation. Wireframes fail to support the task. 60
Adherence to Constraints Flawless adherence to grayscale, single-font, structural constraints. Mostly follows constraints, but minor visual styling slipped in. Relied too heavily on visual styling rather than structure. Ignored constraints (used color, images, etc.). 40
