Project 02: Building the System

Components, Variables & Design Systems

Canvas Assignment Settings:

  • Points: 200
  • Submission Type: Online
    Website URL / Figma Link + File Upload
  • Allowed File Types: .pdf (for Design System Documentation)

Project Overview

Great interfaces are not built one screen at a time—they are built from systems of reusable parts. Modern product designers rarely create every button, form field, or navigation element independently. Instead, they construct flexible component libraries governed by shared rules, allowing entire products to scale efficiently while remaining visually and functionally consistent.

For this project, introduced during Tuesday Lecture and developed throughout Thursday Labs, you will transform the structural wireframes created in Project 1 into a fully functioning design system. Rather than designing individual screens, you will build the reusable foundation that could generate hundreds of screens through consistent components, variables, and documentation.

Using Figma’s component system, Auto Layout, Variables, and Dev Mode documentation, you will construct a scalable UI library capable of supporting your interaction flow while following accessibility and professional handoff standards.

Pillars Addressed: Systems, Tools, Future-Focused Professional

Course Outcomes: Construct reusable component libraries, implement design tokens and variables, and document scalable design systems for collaborative production.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this project, you will be able to:

  1. Transform interface elements into reusable components and component sets.
  2. Build and organize a scalable design token system using variables for color, typography, spacing, and sizing.
  3. Apply Auto Layout and responsive constraints to create flexible interface components.
  4. Document a professional design system suitable for developer handoff and future expansion.

Lecture vs. Lab Execution Schedule

  • TUE Lecture Briefing: Atomic Design methodology, component architecture, token systems, accessibility standards, design system governance, and developer workflows.
  • THU Lab Execution: Component construction in Figma, Auto Layout implementation, variable creation, variant management, accessibility testing, and documentation for developer handoff.

Step-by-Step Instructions

The Scenario

Continue developing the application you designed in Project 1. Rather than creating additional screens, your task is to build the reusable system that powers those screens.

Imagine your application has grown from a small prototype into a product used by thousands of people. A development team now needs a professional design system that allows them to build new features while maintaining consistency across the interface.

Part 1: Design Tokens & Variables

(Lecture Theory / Lab Construction)

Establish the foundational rules that govern your interface.

Create variables (design tokens) for:

  • Primary, secondary, and semantic colors
  • Typography hierarchy
  • Spacing scale
  • Corner radius values
  • Elevation or shadow styles (if applicable)

Use clear naming conventions that could be understood by another designer or developer.

Part 2: Component Library

(Lab Execution)

Convert the recurring interface elements from Project 1 into reusable components.

Your library should include, at minimum:

  • Buttons
  • Text inputs
  • Navigation elements
  • Cards or containers
  • Icons or icon placeholders
  • Form controls (checkboxes, toggles, radio buttons, etc.)

Each component should be constructed using Auto Layout whenever appropriate.

Part 3: Variants & Component States

(Lab Execution)

Expand your components into interactive systems by creating multiple states.

Examples include:

  • Default
  • Hover
  • Focus
  • Pressed
  • Disabled
  • Error / Success (where appropriate)

Use component properties and variants to minimize duplication and maximize flexibility.

Part 4: Design System Documentation

(Lecture Review / Lab Documentation)

Create a concise documentation page within your Figma file that explains how another designer or developer should use your system.

Include:

  • Naming conventions
  • Token organization
  • Component anatomy
  • Usage guidelines
  • Accessibility considerations
  • Developer notes or specifications

Think of this as the instruction manual for your design system.

Submission Requirements

Please submit the following:

  1. Design System Documentation (PDF): Export a document containing your component inventory, design tokens, naming conventions, and usage guidelines.
  2. Figma Link (URL): A link to your completed Figma file containing your organized component library, variables, variants, and documentation. (Crucial: Ensure link sharing is set to “Anyone with the link can view.”)

Grading Rubric (200 Points)

Criteria Excellent (100%) Proficient (80%) Developing (60%) Needs Work (0–50%) Pts
Design Tokens & Variables Comprehensive, well-organized variable system with clear naming and excellent scalability. Complete token system with minor inconsistencies. Variable system is incomplete or inconsistently organized. Little or no evidence of a reusable token system. 50
Component Library Components are reusable, logically organized, and built with excellent Auto Layout practices. Functional component library with minor structural issues. Components function but show inconsistent construction or organization. Components are missing, duplicated, or poorly constructed. 60
Variants & System Flexibility Components include robust variants and state management demonstrating scalable thinking. Most components include useful variants and states. Limited use of variants or inconsistent implementation. Components remain static with little evidence of reusable system thinking. 50
Documentation & Professional Handoff Documentation is complete, organized, accessible, and ready for developer collaboration. Documentation communicates the essentials with minor omissions. Documentation lacks clarity or important information. Documentation is incomplete or missing. 40

03 Design Technology II/07 Project 03.ht.content:
Project 03: Designing Behavior

Motion, Interaction & Prototype Choreography

Canvas Assignment Settings:

  • Points: 200
  • Submission Type: Online
    Website URL / Figma Link + File Upload
  • Allowed File Types: .mp4 (Prototype Walkthrough), .pdf (Motion Documentation)

Project Overview

Static interfaces communicate structure—but interactive interfaces communicate behavior. Every button press, transition, loading indicator, and animation teaches users how a system responds. Well-designed motion reduces cognitive load, reinforces hierarchy, and provides meaningful feedback, helping users understand both where they are and what happens next.

For this project, introduced during Tuesday Lecture and refined throughout Thursday Labs, you will transform the design system created in Project 2 into a fully interactive prototype. Rather than focusing on visual aesthetics alone, you will choreograph how your interface behaves across time through micro-interactions, transitions, and state changes.

Using Figma’s prototyping tools, Smart Animate, interactive components, and motion principles, you will design an experience that feels responsive, intuitive, and intentional. Every animation should serve a purpose—guiding attention, communicating system status, or reinforcing user actions.

Pillars Addressed: Systems, Cognition, Research, Creative Confidence

Course Outcomes: Create interactive prototypes, implement motion as a communication tool, and evaluate interface behavior through usability testing and iterative refinement.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this project, you will be able to:

  1. Apply motion principles to communicate feedback, hierarchy, and state changes.
  2. Build interactive component behaviors using variants and prototype connections.
  3. Design multi-screen transitions that reinforce user understanding and navigation.
  4. Evaluate and refine interface behavior through usability testing and accessibility considerations.

Lecture vs. Lab Execution Schedule

  • TUE Lecture Briefing: Motion theory, temporal design, easing, interaction feedback, accessibility considerations, and cognitive load.
  • THU Lab Execution: Smart Animate implementation, interactive component states, prototype construction, usability testing, motion refinement, and video documentation.

Step-by-Step Instructions

The Scenario

Continue developing the application you designed in Projects 1 and 2.

Your design system now contains reusable components, but it still behaves like a collection of static screens. Your task is to bring the interface to life by designing meaningful interactions that communicate with the user through motion and feedback.

Imagine your prototype will be demonstrated to stakeholders who need to understand not only what the interface looks like, but how it behaves during real-world use.

Part 1: Interactive Component Behaviors

(Lecture Theory / Lab Construction)

Transform your static components into interactive elements by creating meaningful behavioral states.

At minimum, demonstrate interactions for:

  • Buttons
  • Form fields
  • Navigation elements
  • Menus or overlays
  • Toggles, switches, or selection controls

Each interaction should clearly communicate user input and system response.

Part 2: Micro-Interactions & Feedback

(Lab Execution)

Design subtle interface behaviors that improve communication between the user and the system.

Include examples such as:

  • Hover feedback
  • Loading indicators
  • Success and error states
  • Form validation
  • Progress indicators
  • Confirmation messages

Every motion decision should improve usability rather than simply decorate the interface.

Part 3: Screen Transitions & User Flow

(Lab Execution)

Connect your screens into a complete interactive experience.

Design smooth transitions that reinforce spatial relationships and guide users through the task established in Project 1.

Consider:

  • Navigation between screens
  • Modal presentations
  • Shared element transitions
  • Overlay behaviors
  • Back navigation
  • Progressive disclosure of information

Your prototype should demonstrate a complete user journey from beginning to end.

Part 4: Motion Evaluation & Accessibility

(Lecture Review / Lab Testing)

Evaluate your prototype through peer usability testing.

Refine your prototype based on observed user behavior and document your revisions.

Consider:

  • Motion timing
  • Ease of navigation
  • Clarity of interaction feedback
  • Reduced-motion accessibility
  • Cognitive load
  • Overall usability

Document the major improvements made after testing.

Submission Requirements

Please submit the following:

  1. Prototype Walkthrough (.mp4): A 2–4 minute screen recording demonstrating your interactive prototype, highlighting key transitions, micro-interactions, and system behaviors while briefly explaining your design decisions.
  2. Motion Documentation (PDF): A concise document illustrating your interaction states, transition logic, usability findings, and revisions made following peer feedback.
  3. Figma Link (URL): A link to your completed interactive prototype containing connected screens, interactive components, and motion behaviors. (Crucial: Ensure link sharing is set to “Anyone with the link can view.”)

Grading Rubric (200 Points)

Criteria Excellent (100%) Proficient (80%) Developing (60%) Needs Work (0–50%) Pts
Interactive Components & States Components demonstrate thoughtful interaction design with robust, clearly communicated state changes throughout the system. Most components include appropriate interactions and state changes with minor inconsistencies. Limited interactive behaviors or inconsistent implementation across components. Components remain largely static with little evidence of interactive design. 50
Motion & User Flow Motion is purposeful, polished, and strengthens navigation, hierarchy, and user understanding across the complete prototype. Motion generally supports usability, though some transitions feel inconsistent or unnecessary. Motion is functional but lacks cohesion or clear communicative purpose. Little or no meaningful motion or prototype flow is demonstrated. 60
Usability & Accessibility Prototype demonstrates strong usability principles, clear feedback, thoughtful accessibility considerations, and meaningful revisions based on testing. Usability is generally effective with some accessibility considerations and evidence of refinement. Limited usability testing or accessibility considerations are evident. Artificial Intelligence (AI) Syllabus Statement

Semester Overview

The semester will be organized around three major projects, each requiring five weeks to complete. Projects will include regular exercises or checkpoints where work will be due; these are to help students progress and develop work toward final reviews. Learning objectives, core concepts, and overall project briefs are shared across studios. Each studio, however, will make very different work because of the diversity of creative perspectives across the faculty and student body. Full project descriptions, rubrics, and schedules are provided by each instructor, typically via Canvas modules.

AI Use in Graphic Design Studios

The role of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in graphic design studios varies by course, depending on learning objectives, course content, and instructor expectations. Some studios may incorporate AI-assisted tools for ideation, image generation, research, or workflow development, while others may limit or prohibit AI use to emphasize foundational skills, creative process, and critical thinking. 

Although learning objectives, core concepts, and overall project briefs are shared across studio sections, each studio will produce distinct outcomes that reflect the diverse creative perspectives of both faculty and students. Detailed project descriptions, grading rubrics, schedules, and AI-use expectations are provided by individual instructors, typically through Canvas modules.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy

Because graphic design spans everything from conceptual ideation to technical execution, this boilerplate is designed to be modular. It uses a "traffic light" framing so you can easily adjust the boundaries based on the specific goals of your course.

Statement of Principle

In the Department of Graphic Design at Iowa State University, we view emerging technologies as powerful tools that can expand, but never replace, human creativity, critical thinking, and ethical responsibility. Graphic design is fundamentally about human communication, empathy, and intent. While Generative AI (such as ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL-E, and Adobe Firefly) can assist in the creative workflow, your value as a designer lies in your unique voice, your iterative process, and your ability to synthesize complex ideas.

Course AI Stance

[Select One: Green / Yellow / Red]

[Instructor Note: Choose the tier that fits your course and delete the other two options before distributing.]

🟢 Option 1: Broad Integration (Green Light)

  • Policy: Generative AI tools are permitted and encouraged in this course as a supplement to your creative process. You may use them for brainstorming, mood-boarding, conceptual ideation, or asset generation.
  • Condition: AI must be treated as a collaborative assistant, not the sole creator. You must document your use of AI (prompts used, platforms utilized) and disclose it in your process books/project presentations. All final compositions must reflect your own significant design intervention, layout, and typographic choices.

🟡 Option 2: Guided/Conditional Use (Yellow Light)

  • Policy: AI tools may be used only for specific assignments or phases of a project as explicitly outlined by the instructor (e.g., using ChatGPT to generate copy for a packaging layout, or Firefly to expand a background image).
  • Condition: Unauthorized use of AI for core creative deliverables (such as generating final logos, complete layouts, or writing design rationale essays) will be considered a violation of academic integrity. When allowed, its use must be explicitly cited.

🔴 Option 3: Traditional/Foundational Focus (Red Light)

  • Policy: The use of generative AI tools is not permitted in this course.
  • Rationale: This course focuses on building foundational skills—such as formal composition, manual typography, grid structures, and technical software mastery—that require hands-on, human execution. Submitting AI-generated imagery, code, or layouts for any assignment will be treated as academic misconduct.

Expectations, Ethics, and Academic Integrity

Regardless of the tier selected above, the following universal rules apply to all graphic design coursework:

  • Ownership and Plagiarism: Presenting AI-generated work as your own completely unaided creation is a violation of the ISU Academic Misconduct policy. If an AI tool is used to generate an asset, that asset must be attributed.
  • The "Copyright" Problem: Current legal frameworks generally dictate that AI-generated imagery cannot be copyrighted, and many AI datasets scrape artists' work without consent. As professional designers in training, you must be aware of the ethical implications of using these tools for commercial client work.
  • Accuracy and Bias: AI tools frequently output "hallucinations" (false facts) and visual biases. If you use AI for research or copywriting, you are entirely responsible for fact-checking and refining the output.
  • Grading Criteria: You are graded on your design process (sketching, iteration, critique, and refinement), not just the final artifact. An AI-generated output that lacks a documented human process will not meet the learning objectives of this department.

University Compliance: Any unauthorized use of AI that violates this syllabus will be reported to the Office of Student Conduct in accordance with Iowa State University’s Academic Integrity regulations.

AI for Design Thinking: Faculty Classroom Activities

Introduction

This document provides a collection of classroom activities designed to help students engage with artificial intelligence as a design thinking partner rather than a replacement for creative practice.

The goal of these activities is not to teach students how to generate finished designs with AI. Instead, they use AI as a tool for expanding the traditional design process: developing empathy, strengthening critique, exploring possibilities, and understanding how design systems function.

Each activity connects to a larger philosophy:

Design is not simply the creation of artifacts — it is the shaping of relationships, experiences, and behaviors.

Professional designers do not only make things. They investigate audiences, evaluate communication, create systems, and make intentional decisions based on context. These activities help students practice those same habits while developing a more critical understanding of where AI can—and cannot—support the design process.

How Faculty Can Use This Document

These activities are designed to be flexible and adaptable across courses, disciplines, and levels of experience. They can be used as:

  • Short classroom exercises (10–30 minutes)
  • Pre-critique preparation activities
  • Project development checkpoints
  • Reflection exercises
  • Studio discussion prompts
  • Assignments integrated into existing projects

Faculty do not need to redesign an entire course to incorporate these activities. Each exercise can be inserted into an existing design workflow at a moment where students would already be asking similar questions.

For example:

  • Use Instant Audience Lab early in a project when students are defining goals, users, and communication strategies.
  • Use AI as a Critique Partner before a studio critique to help students arrive prepared with questions and revision ideas.
  • Use System Generator during concept development when students need to move beyond individual solutions toward scalable design systems.

A Different Model for AI in Design Education

Many conversations about AI in design focus on speed, automation, or production output. These activities intentionally shift that conversation.

Rather than asking:

“How can AI make the artifact faster?”

Students are encouraged to ask:

“How can AI help me think more deeply about the problem?”

This approach positions AI as:

  • A research assistant that helps uncover perspectives
  • A critique partner that challenges assumptions
  • A systems collaborator that helps explore relationships and variation

The designer remains responsible for interpretation, judgment, authorship, and decision-making.

The Progression

Together, these activities follow a progression that mirrors professional design practice:

1. Audience

Who is it for?

Students develop empathy and learn to evaluate whether their design communicates effectively to specific people.

2. Critique

Is it working?

Students practice evaluating design from multiple perspectives and identifying opportunities for refinement.

3. System

How does it scale?

Students move beyond individual artifacts and begin designing rules, relationships, and frameworks that can generate multiple outcomes.

Implementation Notes

These activities work best when AI outputs are treated as starting points for discussion, not authoritative answers. Encourage students to question AI-generated responses:

  • What assumptions is this making?
  • What perspectives are missing?
  • What information is inaccurate or oversimplified?
  • What decisions still require human judgment?

The purpose is not to reduce the designer’s role, but to strengthen the designer’s ability to think critically, communicate intentionally, and make informed decisions in an increasingly complex creative environment.

Activity 1: Instant Audience Lab

Design Begins with People

Core Principle

Design is communication. Before we can evaluate whether something is visually successful, we have to understand who it is speaking to. Audience is often discussed in broad, abstract terms—“design for your users”—without giving students practical ways to imagine those users.

This activity uses AI to rapidly generate believable audience perspectives that students can use to test assumptions, identify blind spots, and strengthen design decisions.

Rather than asking AI to design, students ask it to help them better understand the people they are designing for.

Learning Outcomes

After completing this activity, students should be able to:

  • Translate abstract audiences into concrete user profiles.
  • Identify how different audiences interpret the same visual communication.
  • Recognize mismatches between design intention and audience perception.
  • Make evidence-informed revisions based on audience feedback.

Faculty Introduction

“One of the biggest challenges for beginning designers is that they often design for themselves. Today we’re going to use AI to quickly generate several audience perspectives so we can test whether our work communicates the way we intend.”

Student Prompt

I am designing a [project type] about [topic].

Generate three detailed audience personas.

For each persona include:

  • age
  • occupation
  • background
  • motivations
  • goals
  • visual preferences
  • prior knowledge
  • accessibility considerations
  • what they might misunderstand

Then explain how each audience would interpret my design.

What would resonate?

What would confuse them?

What questions would they still have?

Reflection Prompt

After reviewing the responses, ask:

  • Which audience surprised you?
  • Which audience understood your design the least?
  • What assumptions did you make that weren’t shared by your audience?
  • What is one revision you would make based on this feedback?

Deliverable (10–15 minutes)

Students submit:

  • Three audience personas
  • Three observations for each persona
  • One design revision they plan to make
  • A short paragraph explaining why that revision improves communication

Why This Works

Instead of asking students to “think about their audience,” this activity gives them multiple concrete viewpoints in minutes. It encourages empathy, improves critique discussions, and helps students recognize that design success depends on communication—not personal preference.

Activity 2: AI as a Critique Partner

Critique as Conversation

Core Principle

Critique is not about determining whether a design is “good” or “bad.” It is an ongoing conversation that reveals strengths, weaknesses, competing priorities, and opportunities for refinement.

AI can support this process by simulating multiple informed perspectives before students enter the classroom. The goal is not to replace peer critique or instructor feedback, but to help students arrive better prepared for meaningful discussion.

Learning Outcomes

Students will:

  • Practice receiving constructive criticism.
  • Compare conflicting viewpoints.
  • Identify recurring patterns across critiques.
  • Develop intentional revision strategies.

Faculty Introduction

“Professional designers rarely receive a single opinion. They receive feedback from clients, users, creative directors, engineers, accessibility experts, marketers, and many others. Today we’ll use AI to simulate those conversations before our in-class critique.”

Student Prompt

Act as an experienced Art Director reviewing this design.

Provide honest feedback focused on:

  • clarity
  • hierarchy
  • concept
  • composition
  • typography
  • audience

Explain both strengths and weaknesses.

Then:

Now review the same design as an Accessibility Specialist.

Then:

Review it again as the intended audience.

Finally:

Compare these critiques.

Where do they agree?

Where do they disagree?

What tensions exist between these perspectives?

What revisions would best satisfy the greatest number of concerns?

Reflection Prompt

Students answer:

  • Which critique felt most valuable?
  • Which perspectives conflicted?
  • Which suggestions aligned with your own thinking?
  • Which suggestions will you ignore—and why?

Deliverable (15–20 minutes)

Students submit:

  • Three critique perspectives
  • One summary of recurring themes
  • One summary of conflicting viewpoints
  • Two planned revisions with justification

Why This Works

Instead of replacing critique, AI helps students practice critique before class begins. Students become more reflective, more articulate, and more prepared to participate in meaningful discussion with peers and instructors.

Activity 3: System Generator

Design Systems Instead of Single Solutions

Core Principle

Strong designers do not simply create isolated artifacts—they build systems capable of producing many coherent outcomes.

Rather than asking AI to generate finished designs, students use it to help define the rules, variables, and constraints that make visual systems scalable and adaptable.

This shifts AI away from idea generation and toward systems thinking.

Learning Outcomes

Students will:

  • Understand the relationship between rules and variation.
  • Distinguish between isolated concepts and scalable systems.
  • Develop repeatable visual frameworks.
  • Explore generative approaches to design.

Faculty Introduction

“Instead of asking AI to create a poster, we’re going to ask it to create the rules that could generate hundreds of posters. Designers build systems—not just artifacts.”

Student Prompt

Create a visual design system for a [poster / publication / identity / campaign] about [topic].

Define:

  • color variables
  • typography variables
  • layout rules
  • imagery rules
  • spacing rules
  • hierarchy rules

Explain why each rule exists.

Then generate five distinct design variations that all follow the same system.

Reflection Prompt

Students answer:

  • Which rules remained constant?
  • Which variables changed?
  • Did the designs still feel related?
  • How could this system expand into a larger identity or campaign?

Deliverable (20–30 minutes)

Students submit:

  • One visual system
  • Three to five generated variations
  • A diagram or list of variables and constraints
  • A short explanation of what creates consistency across all outcomes

Why This Works

Students begin thinking like systems designers instead of artifact makers. The exercise naturally connects AI prompting with computational design, generative typography, identity systems, responsive design, and creative coding. It also creates a direct bridge to later work in p5.js, algorithmic design, and responsive web systems.

The Overall Arc

These build on one another as a progression rather than feeling like three disconnected AI activities:

Stage Design Question AI Role Student Learns
1. Audience Who is this for? Research & empathy partner Human-centered design
2. Critique Is it working? Reflective dialogue partner Iteration & evaluation
3. Systems How does it scale? Systems thinking partner Rules, variation & generative design

The sequence reinforces the philosophy outlined: design is not the production of isolated artifacts, but the creation of relationships, behaviors, and systems. It also reframes AI as a tool for inquiry and reflection.
